title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a fake interview between two real, named public figures and attach their credibility to an unlicensed investment platform. The failure is not inside a legitimate AI product's deployment pipeline, it is the deliberate misuse of AI tools to produce convincing synthetic media for fraudulent purposes. The content was designed to bypass the ordinary skepticism a reader might apply to an unknown source by substituting recognizable, trusted identities.

The scale reported by ASIC, tens of thousands of scam removals in a single year, shows this is a pattern rather than an isolated case. What would have been required to catch any individual instance is a reader independently verifying the financial services license of the promoted platform through an official register, or confirming the interview existed through the ABC's own channels. Neither the polish of the content nor the familiarity of the names involved was a reliable signal of legitimacy.

What is not established is whether specific AI companies or platforms were found to have directly enabled these scams, or what legal consequences, if any, followed from the fabricated content about Boulder Sparhaven.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock engaged in a heated confrontation represents a growing type of scam using artificial intelligence. The fabricated interview promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, and never actually occurred. This scheme exemplifies how scammers increasingly use AI-generated deepfakes and convincing fake content to deceive investors, making fraudulent opportunities appear legitimate and trustworthy.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission data reveals these investment scams are becoming more prevalent and sophisticated. Last year, the regulator removed 19,400 scams overall, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated figures. ASIC warns consumers to verify financial services licenses independently through official registers and advises that familiar branding or polished content does not guarantee legitimacy. Kohler has called for heavy fines against platforms and AI models that enable these scams.
